title: Results on 2026
text:
Calibration


The average gap between predicted and actual frequency is 0.4 percentage points or less for every pitch type. The pitcher’s mix alone (blue) is overconfident at high probabilities; the model (red) fixes that.

title: Results on 2026
text:
Per pitcher

Of the 468 pitchers with 500+ pitches in 2026, the model beats the baseline for all of them and beats the best mix for 98%.

Biggest gains: Ryan Rolison, Yusei Kikuchi and Shane Baz, all deep repertoires where count and sequence matter a lot.
Where it doesn’t help: John King, Josh Hader and Pete Fairbanks, mostly two-pitch relievers whose mix already says nearly everything. The model loses a little by applying league-wide count habits that don’t fit them.

title: Results on 2026
section: An idea that didn’t hold up
text:
An idea that didn’t hold up
On 2025, a family-first model (predict fastball / breaking / offspeed, then the pitch from his mix) looked better for pitchers whose pitch labels had changed. I wrote “use it for relabeled pitchers” into the test plan before scoring 2026. On 2026 it was worse for those pitchers (1.275 vs. 1.253 log loss, interval +0.012 to +0.032), so it was dropped. The 2025 edge came from about 2,000 pitches. The family view stays in the report because it’s what a hitter prepares for.

title: Results on 2026
text:
Limitations

Pitch type only, not location.
Public data only: no catcher targets, game plans or scouting reports.
Pitch labels come from Savant’s classifier, and relabels are only partly repaired.
xgboost’s interactions aren’t directly readable. The logistic model is the one to explain; the trees show interactions add about as much again.

title: Methods, in plain language
text: For each pitch, give a probability for each of eight pitch types using only what was known before the pitch: who’s pitching and batting, the count, the previous pitches and what happened on them, runners, outs, score, inning, times through the order and pitch count.

title: Methods, in plain language
text: For each pitch, give a probability for each of eight pitch types using only what was known before the pitch: who’s pitching and batting, the count, the previous pitches and what happened on them, runners, outs, score, inning, times through the order and pitch count.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Step 1: Know the pitcher
Most of a pitch’s predictability is the pitcher himself. The model starts from his pitch mix, built in three layers:

Prior mix. His pitches from earlier seasons, with last season counting most (two seasons back counts a quarter as much). It’s shrunk toward the league mix for pitchers with the same throwing hand and role: each pitcher starts with 100 pitches’ worth of league average. With 3,000 pitches of history that barely matters. With 30 it decides almost everything. This is empirical Bayes, and it stops the model from saying “0% curveball” because a rookie hasn’t thrown one yet.
Current form. The prior mix updated with his pitches this season, through his previous game only. Pitch mixes change a lot from year to year, and a pitcher’s first few outings already show how.
Platoon tilt. His usual split against left- vs. right-handed hitters.

Before the prior mix is built, Savant relabels are repaired: if a pitch he used to throw has vanished this season while a new one with the same velocity and movement has appeared, his history of the old label is credited to the new one.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Step 2: Know the situation
Two models take his mix as their starting point and learn how the situation moves him away from it.

Multinomial logistic regression. One equation per pitch type turns the situation into a probability for each pitch. His mix enters as a fixed offset, so the model never relearns who throws what. Its coefficients are league-wide answers like “with two strikes, pitchers go to their breaking ball more often than usual.” A ridge penalty keeps the many dummy variables (count × handedness, previous pitch × its result) from overfitting.
Gradient boosting (xgboost). Trees fitted with the same starting point, so they can find interactions without anyone writing them by hand. For example: two strikes, a same-handed hitter, and a slider that just got a whiff.

A batter layer adds how pitchers have attacked this hitter compared with what their own mixes predicted, using earlier games only and shrunk toward zero for hitters with little history.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
Step 3: Test honestly

Time split. Train on 2023-24, tune every setting on 2025, then refit on 2023-25 and score 2026 once.
Pre-registration. The models, metrics and decision rules for 2026 were committed to the repo before 2026 was scored.
Metrics. Log loss is the headline because it rewards honest probabilities and heavily punishes confident misses. Top-1 accuracy is easier to explain but flatters pitchers who throw one pitch 60% of the time, so it’s always shown next to the baseline. Calibration plots check that “40%” means 40%.
Uncertainty. 95% intervals come from 500 bootstrap resamples of whole games, because pitches within a game aren’t independent.

title: Methods, in plain language
text:
What the model can’t know
It predicts pitch type, not location, and location is half of a pitcher’s decision. Public data shows where the ball ended up, not where the catcher set up, so the report shows location as density maps that blend intent with missed spots. The model doesn’t see the catcher, the game plan or the scouting report on the hitter. Expect real but modest gains over a pitcher’s own mix: pitchers are paid to be unpredictable.

title: Data and cleaning
text:
Cleaning steps
Each step is a SQL view in DuckDB with a row count logged after it (full cleaning log).

Regular season only. Spring training, exhibitions and the postseason are dropped using Savant’s game_type.
Duplicates removed. If a day is re-pulled (Savant revises recent data), the newest copy of each pitch wins.
Impossible rows removed. Missing pitcher or batter, or a count or out total that can’t happen. None were found.
Position players pitching removed (about 9,500 pitches), using primary position from the MLB Stats API rather than a velocity guess. Two-way players like Ohtani are kept.
Eight pitch groups. Four-seam, sinker, cutter, slider, sweeper, curveball (curve, knuckle curve, slurve, slow curve), changeup and splitter (splitter, forkball).

Pitches outside those groups (automatic balls from pitch-clock violations, pitchouts, knuckleballs, eephus pitches) stay in the table so they still count as “the previous pitch” for the next one, but they’re never prediction targets.

title: Data and cleaning
text:
The leakage guard
The data dictionary documents all 120 Savant fields and 15 derived ones. Each is tagged with when it becomes known:

Before the pitch: count, runners, outs, score, handedness, times through the order. Only these can be model inputs.
After the pitch: velocity, spin, location, result. Used in the report, never as an input for the same pitch.
Future: Savant includes pitcher_days_until_next_game, which is only knowable in hindsight. It’s tagged and never used.

title: Data and cleaning
text:
Known data issues

Savant relabels pitches. Some pitchers’ sliders became sweepers, or four-seamers became sinkers, between seasons. That’s a label change, not a new pitch. The pipeline detects and repairs clean relabels by matching velocity and movement, but only partly. 19 pitcher-seasons flipped their slider/sweeper split by 50+ points.
Times through the order comes from Savant’s n_thruorder_pitcher. It agrees with a version derived from the pitcher’s own batter count 99.8% of the time.

title: Predicting the next pitch
text: Given the count, the previous pitches, who’s batting and the game situation, what does this pitcher throw next? I built a model that answers that with honest probabilities, tested it once on a season it had never seen, and turned it into the kind of pitcher-vs-batter advance report a coaching staff could use.

Every step in the table is a real improvement: the 95% bootstrap interval for each difference, resampling whole games, excludes zero. The model beats the baseline for all 468 pitchers who threw 500+ pitches in 2026, and it’s well calibrated: when it says 40% slider, sliders come about 40% of the time.

title: Predicting the next pitch
text:
What makes it credible

A hard baseline. Every model has to beat the pitcher’s own pitch mix, shrunk toward similar pitchers for thin samples, not a league-average strawman.
A time split. Train on 2023-24, tune on 2025, test once on 2026. Never a random split, because the model’s job is predicting the future.
A pre-registered test. The 2026 test plan, including the rule for which model the app uses, was committed to the repo before 2026 was scored. One idea I liked (a family-first model for relabeled pitches) looked good on 2025, failed on 2026, and was dropped.
Leakage guards. Every field is tagged by when it becomes known. Pitcher mixes use only games before the one being predicted.

title: Predicting the next pitch
text:
Where it helps most
The model earns its keep where pitchers move furthest from their usual mix: hitter’s counts (3-0, 3-1, 2-0) and two-strike counts (0-2, 1-2). In the 2025 tuning season, after a swing-and-miss, pitchers threw the same pitch again 49% of the time, against 32% if you only knew their mix. The logistic model predicted 50%.

title: Sample advance report
text:
How to read it

Predicted next pitch. The model’s probabilities for a chosen situation (here a 1-2 count, previous pitch unknown), shown only for pitches he actually throws to this side. The tick marks his usual mix against this side, so the gap between bar and tick is what the situation adds. When earlier pitches aren’t specified, the prediction averages over his likely previous pitches rather than pretending there weren’t any.
Mix by count. What he actually threw to left-handed hitters in each count in 2026, with the number of pitches on the right. Small cells are noisy.
Model by count. The model’s fastball / breaking / offspeed split and two most likely pitches in each count. This is the family view a hitter prepares for.
Where his pitches go. Location density by pitch type, from the catcher’s view. Public data shows where the ball ended up, not where the catcher set up, so the shading blends where he aims with how often he misses.
Expected outcomes by pitch type. xwOBA for the hitter against each of the pitcher’s pitch types (from pitchers of the same hand), and for the pitcher throwing them to this side, over 2025-26. Values are shrunk toward league average so small samples don’t mislead; the plate appearances are shown on each bar.
Arsenal and platoon splits. Velocity, movement, whiff and chase rates by pitch, and each player’s splits by handedness.
